title: submerged ice age coast reveals ancient aboriginal landscape
dek: diving rangers uncovered stone tools near a former river and a freshwater spring, supporting the sea floor holds deep cultural layers.
body: beneath the turquoise waters off western australia, a rocky hill once overlooked a winding river channel. today, that hill stands as a silent sentinel over a drowned landscape, its base carpeted in sand and sea grass. archaeologists working with murujuga rangers descended into the blue, finding stone artefacts resting on the ancient seabed. each piece tells a quiet story of people who once walked this now-submerged ground.

the discoveries cluster around two distinct features. one site sits near a freshwater spring that would have been a lifeline for mobile communities. the other rests beside a hilltop vantage point overlooking a former river course. these were not random camps; they were places of choice, where water and visibility shaped daily life. the artefacts lie where they fell, preserved in the quiet dark of the ocean.

the research team, from flinders university and partners, included murujuga rangers who received scientific diving training. their local knowledge proved essential, guiding the divers to spots where the sea floor yielded its secrets. the collaboration model shows how indigenous expertise and scientific methods can move together under the waves. the rangers' presence turned a standard survey into a partnership of care and curiosity.

analysis of the stone tools reveals an unexpected detail. some were made from material sourced near rosemary island, roughly 23 kilometres from where they were found. this suggests people deliberately selected and carried stone across a landscape that is now underwater. the movement of raw material points to planning, to a sense of place, and to connections that stretched across a terrain that no longer exists above the tide.

the sites were submerged at least 9,000 years ago, yet the artefacts may be far older. rising seas after the last ice age drowned more than two million square kilometres of australia's continental shelf, erasing coastlines that had been occupied for millennia. these underwater sites are not isolated curiosities; they are part of a wider cultural landscape, a submerged network of places once walked by the ngarda-ngarli people.

the work builds on the deep history of sea country project, which has been mapping australia's drowned past since 2020. each new find adds a chapter to a story that began at least 50,000 years ago, when the ngarda-ngarli people first cared for this country. the sea did not erase that care; it simply moved the landscape beneath the waves. protecting these submerged places is now a matter of preserving the continuity of a living culture.

professor jonathan benjamin, the study's lead author, puts it simply: these landscapes did not simply disappear when they were flooded. they remain part of country, preserving evidence of lives, knowledge, and connection. we are only beginning to understand the scale of australia's submerged heritage. each discovery reveals another thread in the deep human story of this continent.
doesnt_show: the exact age of the artefacts has not been determined, and no organic material suitable for direct dating was reported
settle: radiocarbon dating of associated organic remains would provide a firm chronology
